_note: Staple grains other than wheat, so a civilisation whose people live on another grain can price its subsistence basket (a civilisation file names its `staple`). Each is a GROWN, land-limited entry shaped like wheat_kg: no material inputs, one hectare-year charged against hectare_land.

millet_kg.basis: per hectare CROPPED with foxtail or broomcorn millet for one growing season, as kg of threshed grain net of seed
millet_kg.yield_basis: GROWN. Dry-farmed foxtail or broomcorn millet of the northern Chinese plains, sown in rows and hoed: on the order of eight hundred to a thousand kilograms of grain per hectare (Hsu Cho-yun, Han Agriculture, 1980; Bray, Science and Civilisation in China vol. 6 pt 2, 1984; archaeobotanical estimates for the Neolithic to Han), so 900 net of the few kilograms of seed held back (conf C). Labour: hoeing and thinning the rows, hand reaping and threshing by flail, about 200 hours per hectare; traditional records run higher, so this is the low end for a skilled Han household with the seed drill (conf C). LAND: the batch is the one hectare-year the basis states, charged at hectare_land's rent like wheat_kg. STRAW: the stalks come off the same hectare as the grain. Pre-modern cereals had a harvest index (grain share of above-ground dry matter) of about a quarter to a third (Donald and Hamblin, 'The biological yield and harvest index of cereals as agronomic and plant breeding criteria', Advances in Agronomy 28, 1976; recalled, not opened), so the stalk is two to three times the grain; a sickle cut leaves stubble and chaff falls at the threshing floor, so a kilogram and a half of straw is taken for each kilogram of grain (conf D, an estimate). Stacking is inside the harvest labour already charged. Straw is a joint output with no reference price, a recorded waste (data/world/waste_heaps.json): it carries no share of the grain's cost, and it is fed to herds and draught animals (95_herds.json, 94_agri_organics_gaps.json).

maize_kg.basis: per hectare CROPPED with maize for one growing season, as kg of shelled grain net of seed
maize_kg.yield_basis: GROWN. Hand-planted maize in hills with the digging stick and no draught animal: traditional milpa returns about a thousand to fifteen hundred kilograms of shelled grain per hectare after shelling and drying losses (Sanders, Parsons and Santley, The Basin of Mexico, 1979; milpa field studies in Guatemala, Scientific Reports 2021, and the review in Frontiers in Agronomy 2023), so 1100 net of seed (conf C). Labour: planting each hill, repeated hoeing, hand harvest, husking and shelling; ethnographic totals vary widely and harvest alone runs to several hundred hours, so about 400 hours per hectare (conf C). LAND: the batch is the one hectare-year the basis states, charged at hectare_land's rent like wheat_kg. STRAW: the stalks come off the same hectare as the grain. Pre-modern cereals had a harvest index (grain share of above-ground dry matter) of about a quarter to a third (Donald and Hamblin, 'The biological yield and harvest index of cereals as agronomic and plant breeding criteria', Advances in Agronomy 28, 1976; recalled, not opened), so the stalk is two to three times the grain; a sickle cut leaves stubble and chaff falls at the threshing floor, so a kilogram and a half of straw is taken for each kilogram of grain (conf D, an estimate).
